claims.text: In disordered, single-phase high-entropy alloy superconductors, Tc and Hc2 are primarily governed by effective valence electron count.
Effective valence electron count modulates electron–phonon coupling strength.
Effective valence electron count modulates the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.
Intrinsic chemical disorder supplies electron-scattering centers.
Disorder-induced scattering can either enhance or suppress Cooper pairing.
Systematic compositional adjustment of Nb, Ti, Zr, Ta, and Hf can tune effective valence electron count while preserving a disordered, single-phase BCC structure.
The Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–Ti high-entropy alloy system can form a BCC structure with random elemental occupation.
Local chemical environments and incipient short-range order in a disordered BCC lattice influence electron scattering.
Scattering associated with the disordered BCC lattice mediates the electron–phonon coupling responsible for superconductivity.
The Nb0.34Ti0.33Zr0.14Ta0.11Hf0.08 alloy has intermediate electron–phonon coupling.
An optimum balance between beneficial pairing interactions and disorder-induced pair breaking maximizes Tc and Hc2.
Tuning effective electron count will cause Tc and Hc2 to increase to an optimum and then possibly decrease because of excessive pair-breaking scattering.
Changes in Tc and Hc2 will correlate with measured indicators of electron–phonon coupling.
Nb0.34Ti0.33Zr0.14Ta0.11Hf0.08 has a superconducting transition temperature near 7.5 K.
Nb0.34Ti0.33Zr0.14Ta0.11Hf0.08 has a high upper critical field.
The proposed mechanism applies only to homogeneous, single-phase solid solutions and may fail in multiphase or partially ordered alloys.
Magnetic pair breaking or intergranular effects may dominate superconductivity in multiphase or partially ordered systems.
